text:
Control can be tested today, pays out at deployment, and an interpretability finding alone stops nothing. Those are real strengths.

But in a control evaluation, a red team produces agents that try to subvert the safeguards. "Measured against a model that is actively trying to defeat it" really means measured against the best attacks humans thought to try. The score holds only while the red team is at least as inventive as the model.

They say control gets better as stakes rise, then concede that a far smarter model might find holes. The second claim is the accurate one: control weakens as the danger grows.

Nor is reading internals just a goal: it already surfaced unverbalized evaluation awareness in a real pre-deployment audit.

Their best point is that a good probe becomes one more monitor inside control. Exactly. Output monitors can be fooled by benign-looking outputs from a model whose reasoning is misaligned; activation monitors look where that reasoning happens. A push on interpretability upgrades control. A push on control does not tell us whether the model is scheming.

They call control the protection for the window "while we build deeper tools." Then the extra push should build them.
